ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: In the attached figure there is a large circle, whose interior is divided by several curved arcs into four congruent spiral-shaped regions. The outer boundary of each region contains an arc on the circumference of the large circle, and the inner boundary consists of two small circular arcs; these small arcs meet near the center of the large circle and connect to the boundary of the large circle. Reasoning: The radius of the large circle is 4 cm, and the four parts are congruent, so the arc length of one part on the outer circumference of the large circle is one quarter of the circumference of the large circle, namely (1/4)(2π·4)=2π. The problem gives that the radius of the arcs used for the division is 2 cm. For one region, its two internal arc edges each connect the common point near the center of the large circle and a point on the large circle; the distance between these two points is 4 cm, exactly the diameter of a small circle with radius 2 cm, so each internal arc is a semicircular arc. The length of a semicircular arc with radius 2 cm is π·2=2π. The perimeter of one region consists of one outer circular arc and two internal semicircular arcs, so the perimeter is 2π+2π+2π=6π cm.

method.method_draft: Inspect the diagram: each region has one arc along the outside of the large circle and two internal curved sides that meet near the center. From the text, the large circle has radius 4 cm and the dividing arcs have radius 2 cm. Use the visual symmetry/congruence to identify that the outside boundary of one part is one fourth of the circumference of the large circle, so its length is (1/4)(2π·4)=2π. Each internal side of that part is a semicircle of radius 2: its endpoints are the center of the large circle and a point on the large circle, separated by 4 cm, which is the diameter of a radius-2 circle. Thus each internal arc has length π·2=2π. Add the three boundary pieces: 2π+2π+2π=6π.
